g.text: '250 OK' is a transfer of ownership - so the order is durably queue, THEN acknowledge
The sending server deletes its copy on that reply. Acknowledge first and lose it, and the email is gone with nobody holding a copy and nobody knowing.
The forty-year-old design, and the four reasons it collapses at this scale
/var/mail/alice/
1735689600.M12345.mailserver <- one email, one file
disk I/O per operation
listing a folder means stat()ing thousands of files; marking one read means rewriting a file.
Every operation is random I/O against a 100-150 IOPS drive.
inode exhaustion
40 billion emails/day is 40 billion files/day. ext4 provisions inodes at format time, so you
hit a ceiling with free bytes remaining - and fsck time scales with inode count.
the mailbox is bound to one machine
a user's mail lives on a specific server, so that server is a single point of failure for that
user, and capacity planning becomes per-user placement.
no search
full-text search means reading every file.
So the design keeps SMTP - the
protocol is fine - and replaces
the storage model entirely:
separate content from
per-recipient state, partition by
user, and put each of the four
data shapes in a store built
for it.
The receive path - and the one line in this module that matters most
sending provider -> our SMTP LB -> SMTP inbound server
1. connection checks: IP on a blocklist? rate-limited? reverse DNS sane?
2. envelope checks: does the recipient exist? SPF pass? size acceptable?
-> reject NOW with 5xx if it fails: the cheapest possible rejection
3. accept the DATA and write it DURABLY to the inbound queue
4. reply 250 OK <- WE NOW OWN THIS MESSAGE
everything below is asynchronous and retryable:
5. virus scan; spam score (content, reputation, DKIM/DMARC verification)
6. store the body content-addressed; store attachments by hash
7. apply the user's filters and rules -> decide the destination folder
8. INSERT the per-recipient metadata row (Inbox, or Junk if spam)
9. enqueue a search-index write
10. push a notification via the real-time server if the user is connected
Under SMTP, replying 250 OK is a TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY: the sending server
deletes its copy and considers the message delivered. Acknowledge and then lose
it, and the email is gone with nobody holding a copy and nobody knowing - the
exact 'data loss is unacceptable' failure.
So the ordering is strict. NOT 'acknowledge, then queue' - a crash there loses
mail silently. And NOT 'process fully, then acknowledge' - spam and virus
scanning would hold the SMTP connection open for seconds, and a slow scanner
would make the sender time out and retry, duplicating the work.
Note also that rejection happens AS EARLY AS POSSIBLE - at connection and
envelope time, before accepting the message body. Rejecting a spam message
after transferring 50 KB wastes bandwidth on every one of them, and at spam
volumes that is most of your inbound traffic.
And duplicate delivery is a ROUTINE EVENT, not an edge case: SMTP retries after
any ambiguous failure, so the same message arriving twice is expected.
Deduplication on (Message-Id, recipient) within a window is essential rather
than optional.
The send path - and the biggest single optimization in the design
client -> LB -> web server
1. authenticate; rate-limit (a compromised account is a spam cannon)
2. validate: size limit, recipient count, header sanity
3. store the body ONCE, content-addressed; attachments by content hash
4. write the sender's own copy into their Sent folder
5. SHORT-CIRCUIT: for recipients on OUR OWN domain, write their
metadata rows directly - no SMTP, no network, no external delivery
6. for external recipients: enqueue onto the outbound queue
-> 202 Accepted
outbound SMTP worker
7. DNS: look up the MX records for the recipient's domain
8. choose a sending IP by reputation and mail class
9. connect, STARTTLS, DKIM-sign, transfer
2xx -> delivered
4xx -> TEMPORARY: requeue with backoff, retry for up to ~3 days
5xx -> PERMANENT: generate a bounce back to the sender
Step 5 is easy to miss and it is the biggest single optimization here. A large
provider's internal mail - one user to another on the same domain - never
touches SMTP at all. It is a metadata row insert: orders of magnitude cheaper
than the external path, and it sidesteps the entire deliverability problem. For
a provider with a billion users, a large fraction of all mail is internal.
Steps 7-9 are why outbound is a WORKER and not a request handler. A destination
server can be down for hours, and SMTP's contract is that a 4xx means 'try again
later' - for up to several days by convention. So the outbound queue holds
messages with a retry schedule spanning DAYS, and there is no request waiting on
any of it. That is a fundamentally different service shape from anything else in
the design.
It is also why outbound capacity CANNOT AUTOSCALE: new sending IPs need weeks of
warm-up, so outbound send capacity is a weeks-ahead provisioning decision rather
than an autoscaling one. An odd constraint in an otherwise elastic system, and
it catches people out.
The read path, for completeness: Redis for recent messages (mail access is
heavily recency-skewed), then headers only from the metadata store, then the
body by content hash for the OPENED message alone - and attachments served
directly from object storage by pre-signed URL, so a 25 MB download never
passes through the API tier.
Six services, and each boundary is forced by a genuine difference
SMTP inbound servers they speak a protocol from 1982 to STRANGERS - hostile, unauthenticated traffic - and their
scaling driver is inbound connection count. Isolating them contains the blast radius of a
protocol-level exploit.
SMTP outbound workers the opposite shape: LONG-LIVED RETRYING connections to third parties over hours or days, with
throughput gated by other people's servers. They also carry the IP reputation, so which IP a
message leaves from is a routing decision that belongs here and nowhere else.
web / API servers stateless HTTPS; the primary client interface
real-time servers they hold STATEFUL WebSocket connections, so they need draining on deploy - and mixing that
into a stateless HTTP tier would impose connection-draining semantics on every release
the search service a completely different engine with an inverted index, whose workload (write-heavy,
read-light) is the inverse of everything else here
mail processing workers the asynchronous work - spam, virus, fan-out, indexing - that must NOT sit between an
inbound connection and its acknowledgement
No component's scaling driver is shared with another's, which is the practical payoff of drawing the boundaries this way.
SMTP has backpressure built in - which is unusual, and worth exploiting rather than working around
421 Service not available / 4xx -> 'retry later'
and well-behaved senders WILL. So under overload the system pushes
legitimate mail back onto the SENDER's queue rather than dropping it.
The number that actually varies is not the diurnal curve: it is SPAM VOLUME,
which is adversarial rather than periodic. A campaign can multiply the inbound
connection rate with no warning, so the inbound tier is sized FOR ATTACK, not
for legitimate mail.
What gets shed under overload, in order
1 search index writes deferred into a backlog. Search goes stale; nothing else is affected, and because
search is read-light, nobody notices quickly.
2 inbound from LOW-REPUTATION IPs get 4xx first. Reputation-weighted admission means legitimate senders are the last
to be throttled.
3 non-urgent outbound bulk and marketing classes are delayed behind transactional mail - the same class
separation that reputation management needs anyway.
4 NEVER shed anything already 250-OK'd that is an ownership promise.
5 NEVER shed inbound from high-reputation senders making Gmail retry is a reputation risk in both directions.
Two scanners behind circuit breakers - and deliberately opposite failure policies
virus scanning -> FAIL CLOSED
deliver to quarantine rather than to the inbox: delivering an
unscanned executable is worse than delaying mail.
spam scoring -> FAIL OPEN
deliver to Inbox with a lower confidence flag: a delayed legitimate
email is worse than an unfiltered spam one.
Two scanners, opposite policies, because the ASYMMETRY OF HARM differs. Naming which way each one fails is the whole point
of putting a circuit breaker around it - a breaker with an unexamined default is just a hidden policy decision.
One inbound message can be five orders of magnitude of writes
one email to a 50,000-member list
= 50,000 metadata inserts + 50,000 index writes
+ 50,000 push notifications - arriving as ONE SMTP transaction
Mitigations: fan out asynchronously in batches rather than synchronously (which
the queue already provides), cap recipients per message, and - the reason
content-addressing matters again - store the body ONCE, so 50,000 copies cost
50,000 small rows rather than 2.5 GB.
Degradation, and note how much SMTP gives for free: the search cluster failing costs only search; real-time servers failing
means clients fall back to polling; the cache failing is slower but correct; outbound workers failing means messages
accumulate in a durable queue with nothing lost; and INBOUND SMTP FAILING MEANS SENDERS RETRY FOR DAYS - so a multi-hour
inbound outage delays mail rather than losing it, which is the single most valuable reliability property the protocol gives
you. Only one failure is deliberately hard: a metadata partition losing quorum makes that partition's users unable to read or
receive, chosen over risking loss. And a non-empty dead-letter queue is an INCIDENT, not a debugging aid, because every
message in it was already acknowledged with 250 OK.
The structural gap worth naming: NO END-TO-END ENCRYPTION. Server-side spam filtering, virus scanning, search indexing and
threading all require reading message content - so E2EE is fundamentally incompatible with most of this design's features,
not merely unbuilt. Alongside it: shared mailboxes do not fit partitioning by user_id (support@company.com read by twelve
people is genuinely shared, and the pseudo-user workaround breaks per-user read state, which is what a shared inbox needs
most); Message-Id deduplication has no defined window (too short duplicates a slow retry, too long grows unboundedly, and
the right value depends on every sending provider's conventions); and unread counters drift, with a recompute that scans a
user's mail - expensive for a million-message mailbox, at a frequency nobody has priced.
